case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 10th, 11th and 12th days of July, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree (F.A.) No. 234 of 2004 with Appeal from Original Decree (F.A.) No. 235 of 2004)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. These two appeals, by leave, are from the common judgment dated the 10th, 11th and 12th days of July, 2006 (separate decrees were drawn and signed) passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree (F.A.) Nos. 234 and 235 of 2004 allowing both the appeals and setting aside the common judgment dated 18.04.2004 (separate decrees were drawn and signed) passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now the joint District Judge), 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit Nos. 100 and 101 of 1997 dismissing both the suits.

2. Facts essential to dispose these civil appeals (CA) are that the appellants as the plaintiffs. filed Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur for pre-emption of the land described in schedule -'A' to the plaint (thereinafter referred to as the suit land) under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage of their land described in schedule 'B' to the plaint.

3. In the plaint, it was stated, inter alia, that the plaintiffs got title and possession in 'B' scheduled land measuring 2.58 acres by way of purchase which were contiguous to the suit land in the southern side. The suit land belonged to defendant No.2, Messer's Solenkhi Ceramic Industries Ltd. which was to the contiguous north and west of the plaintiffs land described in schedule- 'B'. Thus, the plaintiffs were Shafi-I-Jar (owner of adjoining immovable property). The plaintiffs got right of way over the suit land from 'B' scheduled land and as such, they were Shafi-I-Khalid to the suit land as well. The plaintiffs were in possession of 'B' scheduled land by purchase from the different owners. Plaintiff No. 1 purchased 18 decimals land out of 15 acres of C.S. and S.A. Plot Nos. 437 and 447 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No.94 and S.A. Khatian No. 219 of muza 563, Mirupr, Police Station-Joydebpur, Gazipur by registered Kabala No. 4849 dated 15.05.1991 from Zakir Hossain Chowdhury, son of late Shahabuddin Chowdhury in the same mouza. Plaintiff No.1 purchased 45 decimals land by Kabala No. 4848 dated 15.05.1991 from Rozina Chowdhury, wife of Zakir Hossain Chowdhury, out of 1.8½ acres land of S.A. Plot Nos. 437 and 447 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 94 and S.A. Plot No. 438 appertaining to S.C. Khatian No. 42, S.A. Khatian No. 149, S.A. Plot No. 443 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 49, S.A. Plot No. 449 appertaining to C.S. Khatian Nos. 49 and 182 and S.A. Plot No. 450 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 1/56, S.A. Khatian No.47. Plaintiff No.1 purchased 33 decimals land out of 1.18½ acres land of those six plots from Raisa Rasul, daughter of the Atiqr Rasul by Kabala No. 4845 dated 15.05.1991 and also 33 decimals land out of those 6 plots from Saila Rasul, daughter of late Atiar Rasl by Kabala No. 4852 dated 15.05.1991. Thuse, plaintiff No. 1 got title and possession in 1.29 acres land in schedule- 'B' by purchase as stated above. Plaintiff No.2, Md. Nurul Islam, also purchased 33 decimals land from Raisa Rasul, daughter of late Atiar Rasul by Kabala No. 4835 dated 15.05.1991, 45 decimals land from Rajina Chowdhury, wife of Zakir Hossain Chowdhury by Kabala No. 4834 on the same day, 33 decimals land from Saila Rasul, daughter of late Atiar Rasul by Kabala No. 4837 of the same dated out of 1.81 acres land in 6 plots, i.e. S.A. Plot Nos. 437 and 447 of C.S. Khatian No. 94, S.A. Plot No. 438 of C.S. Khatian No. 42 and S.A. Khatian No. 149, S.A. Plot No. 449 of C.S. Khatian No. 49 and 182 and C.S. and S.A. Plot No. 450 of C.S. Khatian No. 1/56 and S.A. Khatian No. 47. Plaintiff No.2 also purchased 18 decimals land from Zakir Hossain Chowdhury, son of late Shahabuddin Chowdhury, out of .75 acre land of S.A. Plot Nos. 437 and 447 of C.S. Khatian No. 94, S.A. Khatian No. 219, R.S. Khatian Nos. 233, 230 by Kabala No. 4839 dated 15.05.1991. Plaintiff No. 2 got title and possession in 1.29 acres land in schedule- 'B'. Plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 together got title and possession in 2.58 acres land in schedule- 'B.

4. In the later part of 1995, the boundary walls were seen to be constructed in the suit land and upon enquiry by the plaintiffs' men, they were informed that the walls were being constructed by defendant No. 2- Company, its owner. On 09.03.1997, at about 4:00 pm, when plaintiff No.2 along with Messers Arshad Hossain and Md. Islami Miah was passing through the suit land, he found one Abu Bakar Siddique living in the newly constructed C.I. sheet but and on query by plaintiff No. 2 as who had raised the but and how he was living there, he (Abu Bakar) disclosed that defendant No.2-Company had sold the suit land to defendant No. 1- Company for a consideration of taka 31,90,000.00 and defendant No.1 had raised the but for him as his caretaker and upon hearing this, plaintiff No. 2 at one by way of immediate demand (Talab-I-Mawasibat) asserted their right pre-empt the suit land in presence and within the hearing of Abu Bakar Siddique from defendant No. 1. On 10.03.1997, plaintiff No. 2 sent his men to the Sub-Registrar's Office at Joydebpur for obtaining certified copy of the deed if any. On getting the certified copy of Kabala No. 3524 dated 07.03.1996, on 18.03.1997, plaintiff No. 2 came to know definitely about the said sale of the suit land to defendant No. 1 by defendant No. 2 for a consideration of taka 31,90,000.00 and registration of the said kabala on 05.03.1997. The defendants and their men intentionally withheld the information about the said sale till registration of the kabala was completed on 05.03.1997. On 19.03.1997 at about 11 am, plaintiff No.2 along with Messer's Arshed Hossain, Md. Ismial Miah and Arman Ali and some other employees of plaintiff No. 1's company went upon the suit land and found Abu Bakar Siddique, caretaker there. Plaintiff No. 2 for self and on behalf of plaintiff No.1 offered to make payment of the whole consideration mentioned in Kabala No. 3524 dated 07.03.1996 to defendant No. 1- Company and again demanded sale of the suit land to them by way of making demand in presence of the witnesses telling that Talab-I-Mowasibat had already been made on 09.03.1997. The plaintiffs were ready to pay the consideration and to pre-empt the suit land as they were experiencing great inconvenience and difficulties due to the purchase of the suit land by defendant No.1, a stranger, having no right and interest and any land contiguous to the suit land and as such, defendant No.1 had no right to retain the said land. The cause of action for the suit arose first on 09.03.1997, when the plaintiffs had come to know for the first time about the sale and made immediate demand and again on 19.031997 when the demand for purchase was made by offering to pay the whole consideration in presence of the witnesses on the suit land and also on 05.03.1997, the date of registration of the sale deed within mouza Mirpur, Police Station- Joydebpur, Gazipur which was within the jurisdiction of the Court. The suit was valued at taka 31,90,000.00 for the purpose of jurisdiction and advalorem court fees of taka 24,750.00 was paid thereon under section 7IV(c) of the Court Fees Act. The plaintiffs were ready to pay to defendant No.1 or deposit in Court the whole amount of consideration of the said kabala or such other sum as the Court might direct, within such time as would be fixed by the Court.

5. The plaintiffs filed another suit being Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 in the same Court on the same date against the same defendants claiming the right of preemption on the same ground as stated in title Suit No. 100 of 1997.

6. Both the suits were contested by defendant No.1 Company purchaser by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suits were malafide, fraudulent, misconceived and were not maintainable in their present form. The suit land was not liable to be preempted under the Muhammedan Law as the same was neither house nor garden nor a small piece of land. Aground of limitation was also taken in the written statements and it was specifically asserted that Talab-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishhad had not been property performed in accordance with the Muhammedan Law. Both the suit lands and the 'B' scheduled land had boundary walls on all sides having only one entrance gate on the eastern boundary wall by the said of the public road known as Kashimpur Road. Neither on 09.03.1997 nor on any other date, plaintiff No.2 with M/s. Ershad Hossain and Md. Ismail Meah passed through or could pass through the suit land as it was surrounded on all sides by a through or could pass through the suit land as it was surrounded on all sides by a boundary wall and had a gate on the eastern side which led to Kashimpur Road and therefore, it was not possible for plaintiff No. 2 or anybody else to enter into or pass through the suit land except through the main entrance gate on the northern side of the eastern wall and the gate remained closed under the supervision of security guard and nobody could enter into the suit land without permission and assistance of the employees and security guards of defendant No. 1 Abu Bakar Siddique was not present in the suit land on 09.03.1997 as he was on leave for one mother from 25.02.1997. The plaintiffs and their men were aware of all the developments from the time of negation between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for sale and execution of the agreement, construction of C.I. sheet but and semi pucca toilets for the employees, execution of tripartite agreement and registration of the sale deeds on 07.03.1996 and M/s. V.K. Ltd. installed and fixed signboard on the eastern wall and installed electric and telephone connection in the suit land on their purchase on 07.03.1996. The lands allegedly purchased by the plaintiffs were bounded on all sides by pucca boundary wall and they were carrying on their manufacturing works therein conveniently and without any inconvenience or difficulty. The suit land was purchased by defendant No.2 from different owners with a view to set up an industry thereon and took loan by mortgaging the land with Sonali Bank and on their failure to repay the loan amount, the bank instituted Mortgage Suit No. 139 of 1990 in Artha Rin Adalat and as defendant No. 2 had no other means to liquidate the liability of the Bank, it entered into an agreement for sale with defendant No.1 and Sonali Bank and ultimately, the entire land was transferred to defendant No.1 through different sale deeds pursuant to the agreement within the knowledge of the plaintiffs. Defendant No.1 sold .42 acre land out of north-eastern part of the suit land to one Md. Serajul Islam, defendant No. 3 through registered kabala dated 16.09.1996 and delivered possession thereof to the purchaser and thus they were in possession of 5.08 acres land out of the total suit land. Neither the suit land nor 'B' scheduled land was specified as required under Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on the count, the suit was also liable to be dismissed.

7. Both the suits were heard analogously and the parties produced evidence, oral and documentary.

8. On conclusion of trial, the learned Subordinate Judge by the judgment and decree dated the 18th day August, 2004 decreed the suits and allowed the prayer for pre-emption. Against the judgment and decree passed in the suits, two separate appeals being F.A. Nos. 234 and 235 of 2006 were preferred before the High Court Division by the contesting defendant and a Division Bench by the impugned judgment and decree allowed the appeals and dismissed the suits. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the High Court Division, the plaintiffs filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 817 and 818 of 2007 before this Court and leave was granted on 27.08.2008 to consider the sub-missions of their learned Counsel as under:

"The learned Counsel appearing for petitioners in the petitioners submits that the present cases involve important question of law including interpretation of several Articles of the Constitution, which are of great public importance, likely to have immense impact on the nation and the society as a whole, that the learned Judges grossly erred in law in holding that Muslim Personal Law of Pre-emption as unconstitutional and offends the provisions of Article 42 of the Constitution, in the face of the fact that section 96(11) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVIII of 1951), which is a protected law by the first Schedule (under Article 47) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and completely turning blind eye to a decision of the Appellate Division in the case reported in 33DLR (AD) 359, This error has vitiated the whole decision and has resulted serious miscarriage of justice, that the learned Judges also erred in opining that the Muslim Law of Pre-emption offends Articles 31 of the Constitution.

He further submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in deciding, erroneously through, a Constitutional question sitting in Civil Appellate Jurisdiction declaring Muslim personal law of Pre-emption, which is in vogue not only in Bangladesh but throughout the Muslim world which is not only unprecedented and unwarranted but also tantamount to exceeding jurisdiction and fraught with the potential of isolating the country from the Muslim World, hence this error committed by the High Court Division deserves consideration and authoritative pronouncement to remove the cloud it has cast.

He submits that the High Court Division erred in law in arriving at a erroneous decision by holding that the right of pre-emption of Shafi-e-jar based on vicinage under the Mohammadan Law is unconstitutional and offends Article 42(1) of the Constitution mainly relying upon a judgment of the Indian supreme Court reported in AIR 1962(SC) 1476, which was based on the secular nature of the Indian Constitution and is never sympathetic to retention of the Muslim Personal Laws in the country. Whereas our constitution vitally differs from the Indian Constitution on this issue. Constitution has expressly protected Muslim Person Laws along with personal laws of other communities but he learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in appreciating the basic difference and was enamored by the so-called secularistic idea and this approach to the case has vitiated the whole decision. He lastly submits that in any view of the matter, the judgment of the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal, but the High Court Division having arrived at an erroneous decision that Muslim Personal Law for Pre-emption is ultra-vires the Constitution and the court as bent on marshaling the evidences to fit in with the erroneous view. The Judges have grossly misinterpreted the statutes and failed to consider that Talab-I Mowsibat and Talab-I-Ishad were duly performed and the suit was filed within one year from the completion of the sale. Moreover, the learned Judges were wrong to hold that the plaintiff-petitioners failed to prove their title over the contiguous land and also the vicinity and the necessity of the suit land. Whereas, the learned Judge ought to have held that the plaintiff-petitioner No.2 is a natural person who confesses Muslim faith and is the beneficiary of the plaintiff-petitioner No.1 company as being the majority shareholder of the company and the trial court decreed the suit deciding all the issues in favour of the plaintiff but the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law and traveled beyond the relevant issues and committed gross illegalities which requires interference by this Court."

9. Mr. T. H. Khan, learned Counsel, for the appellants, has reiterated the submissions on which leave was granted. Therefore, we do not restate the submission made by him.

10. Mr. Tabarak Hossain, learned Counsel, for respondent No.1, on the other hand, has supported the impugned judgment and order.

11. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that it decreed the suits on the findings, inter alia, that the plaintiffs proved that they were the owners of 'B' scheduled land which is contiguous to the suit land and therefore, they were entitled to filed the suit for pre-emption as Shafi-I-Jar; that the plaintiffs failed to prove that they had a path way on the suit land for engross and outgress from 'B' scheduled land; that the suits were filed well within the period of limitation; that the plaintiffs proved their case of Talab-I-Mowasibat and Talab-I-Ishad.

<u>12. From the impugned judgment, it appears that for the first time, a new point was raised before the High Court Division to the effect that the law of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law, particularly, Shafi-I-Jar, that is, pre-emption on the ground of vicinage was ultra vires the Constitution as the same offended articles &92), 28(1), 31 and 42 of the Constitution. We feel it necessary to keep on record that in the Memorandum of appeal, the ground as to the vires of the law of preemption on the ground of vicinage under the Muhammedan Law being violative of those articles was not taken. The High Court Division on consideration of article 28(1) of the Constitution came to the finding that "Muslim Law" of preemption "so far it is applicable to the urban property" was discriminatory and also affected the secular nature of the Republic. Therefore, Muslim Law of pre-emption so far as it relates to the town property was void as it discriminated between a citizen and a citizen on the ground of religion and faith inasmuch as under section 24 of the Act a Non-Muslim contiguous land owner could not maintain an action for preemption, but a Muslim could. Considering article 42 with article 31 of the Constitution, the High Court Division held that the privilege available to Muslim citizen for preemption as Shafi-I-Jar adversely affected the interest of both the vendor and the vendee and thus it was not only discriminatory and violative of article 42(1) of the Constitution, also opposed to the principles of justice, equity and good conscience and therefore, the right of pre-emption as Shafi-I-Jar was void.</u>

13. Admittedly the suits were filed for pre-emption of the suit land claiming it as agricultural land, so there was no question of deciding the voidess of the right of pre-emption of non-agricultural land as Shafi-I-Jar under the Muhammedan Law, but the High Court Division declared that the Law of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law so far as it relates to the town property was void.

<u>14. The High Court Division further found that the restriction in transferring the land by the owner other than to the contiguous land owner was an unreasonable restriction within the meaning of article 42(1) of the Constitution, as the privilege conferred upon a Muslim citizen to invoke the law of preemption as Shafi-I-Jar imposed a restriction upon a citizen either in the matter of acquiring a property or holding property and/or in the matter of transfer of the property and the same thus offended the said article and article 31 of the Constitution. The High Court Division went further to say that if there was no law of preemption, a vendor could be entitled to sell his property to anybody at a reason-able price that could be settled between him and the purchaser, but because of the law or preemption "the right to terms for property freely was clearly restricted by the law of preemption which in many case resulted in repression of the price which the vendor could otherwise be able to get for his property." The High Court Division further held that it also imposed a restriction on a citizen to acquire a property. The High Court Division further held that right of preemption as Shafi-I-Jar adversely affected the vendor in that he could not get the proper price from a prospective buyer as the prospective buyer would be always under threat of losing his newly acquired property through an action of preemption. Therefore, according to the High Court Division, the privilege available to a Muslim citizen as a Shafi-I-Jar adversely affected the interest of both the vendor and the vendee and in a country, where there was explosion of the population and tremendous pressure on land the attempt to keep the land in the hands of the contiguous land holder could not be justified. Moreover, this right of contiguous land owner also offends the rule against perpetuity as the lands are not allowed to change hands freely. As a result, the possibility of development of land and improvement of quality in the life of the community suffers. The High Court Division observed that in the context of present day reality and the globalization of the world, the restriction imposed on transfer of property and/or acquiring property by the law of preemption such as Shafi-I-Jar could not be encouraged and such a restriction impended national interest.</u>

<u>15. The High Court Division also found the suits misconceived and non-maintainable as plaintiff No.1 being a juridical per-son was incapable of professing any faith. Therefore, it could not file the suit for pre-emption under the Mohammadan Law. The High Court Division further held that Muslim Law was the personal law of the "Musalaman" and the personal law of the vendor governs a transaction of sale of immovable property and not that of the vendee for the purpose of determining the right of shufa and when the vendor of an immovable property is a company "the Muslim law cannot have any manner of application to that transaction." The High Court Division further held that plaintiff No.2 was a natural person, but the suit as framed could not be maintained by him solely as there was no averment in the plaint "nor in evidence to show contiguity of his land with the suit land." The High Court Division also held that the suits were barred by limitation as the demands for preemption were made long after the sale was completed under the Muslim Law. In the instant case, admitted position was that the agreement, exhibit- 'A' was executed on 16.08.1995 and part payment was made on that date and physical possession of the suit land was also handed over to the vendee and on receipt of full consideration, the sale deed was executed and presented for registration on 07.03.1996 and the suit was filed on 30.06.1997, i.e. much beyond the period of limitation. In holding so, the High Court Division relied upon the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed @ Tofa Mia and others-Vs- Abdul Latuf Bhuiyan being dead, his heirs Asia Khatun and others 33, DLR (AD) 359.</u>

16. The High Court Division further held that the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff were the owners of 'B' scheduled land was erroneous and against the weight of evidence; the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove the performance of the Talabs which was fatal for them. It further held that those were very much important legal issues but in holding that the plaintiff proved the making of Talab-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishad, the Court not only ignored these legal aspects of the case, but "is also found to be guilty of misreading and/or misappreciating the evidence and materials on record." The High Court Division further held that plaintiff No.1 was a company and plaintiff No.2 was the Managing Director of that company, if the company wanted to pre-empt the suit land as the contiguous land owner, it was incumbent upon the plaintiffs to show that they were authorized to exercise that right by the Memorandum of Association of the company; neither the Memorandum of Association was produced before the Court nor any Board resolution was produced to show that the company ever decided to buy the suit land. Besides, there was also no resolution showing that plaintiff No.2 was authorized to file the suits on behalf of the company as well. It further observed that plaintiff No.1 was not a natural person and it acts through its Board of Director, if the company wanted to buy the suit land, it must be decided in a Board meeting, but no resolution of such Board meeting was produced. There was also no averment in the plaint to that effect nor there was any oral or documentary evidence that PW1 as the Managing Director of plaintiff-company was authorized to exercise such authority on behalf of the company. The plaintiffs filed the suits for pre-emption as Shafi-I-Jar, but admittedly, the suit land was a vast track of land consisting of about 6 acres. Though the suit land was recorded as agricultural land but the admitted position was that in the vicinity of the suit land industrial units were established and the plaintiffs themselves set up two industrial undertaking on 'B' scheduled land. Thus by now the land has been changed into industrial land. It was also evident from exhibit-'A' that the land was bought by the vendor to set up industry. The object behind the application of the law of pre-emption of the land sold was to safeguard the privacy of Muslim families, right of preemption, therefore, could not be enforced in the case of commercial lands, because in such cases the question of disagreeable neighbor does not arise.

17. The High Court Division further found that the plaintiffs were the owners of 2.58 acres land, whereas they instituted the suit to preempt 8.69 acres land as Shafi-I-Jar. The claim of the right of preemption on the ground of vicinage alone will not lie in the case of large estates and was available only when either houses or small holdings was transferred; preemption under the Mohammedan Law was to prevent the inconvenience which might result from the introduction of a disagreeable stranger as a co-partner or as a near neighbor, its object was to prevent possible vexation arising from a disagreeable neighbor.

18. The High Court Division also found that Title Suit No. 101 of 2007 was not maintainable on the separate ground that it was in the pleading and in evidence that part of the suit land, i.e. .42 acre land was sold to one Md. Serajul Islam by defendant No.1, by a registered kabala on 16.09.1996, but that land was also included in the suit land. There was no pleading or evidence that talabs were made in respect of said 42 decimals land.

19. The plaintiffs also failed to demarcate and identify the lands of Title Suit No.101 of 2007 and also failed to establish the contiguity with 'B' scheduled land, on top of that the plaintiffs failed to comply with the provisions of Order VII, rule 3 of the Code.

20. The High Court Division found that the law of preemption as recognized in the Mohammedan Law was not "quaranik law." or "Islamic Institution" and it emanated partly from Arab culture and partly from customs. It went further saying that the "Muslim law of pre-emption" was found in common use among the Muslims not as their personal law but on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience and among the Non-Muslim as customary law during the British rule in this sub-continent. The High Court Division also found that the basis of the law of Shafi-I-Jar under the Mohammedan Law based on the saying of the great prophet that "neighbor has a right superior to that of a stranger in the land adjacent to him."

21. In view of the findings of the High Court Division as noted down hereinbefore and the leave granting order, the first and the foremost question that has to be decided in these appeals is whether the right of pre-emption as available under the Mohammedan Law as a Shafi-I-Jar is ultra vires the Constitution being violative of article 42(1) read with article 31 of the Constitution as found by the High Court Division, because if it is found that the High Court Division is correct in holding the above view then it would not be necessary to go into the merit of the suits.

22. Article 42 of the Constitution reads as follows:

"42. (1) Subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property, and no property hall be compulsorily acquired, nationalized or requisitioned save by authority of law.

(2) A law made under clause (1) of this article shall provide for the acquisition, nationalization or requisition with compensation and shall fix the amount of compensation or specify the principles on which, and the manner in which, the compensation is to be assessed and paid; but no such law shall be called in question in any court on the ground that any provision of the law in respect of such compensation is not adequate."

<u>23. A reading of sub-article (1) of article 42 shows that subject to any restrictions imposed by law, a citizen shall have the fundamental right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of his property. The phraseology used in this sub-article, namely, "any restrictions imposed by law" is to be interpreted vary carefully and in interpreting this phraseology, we have to take into consideration article 31 of the Constitution. But firstly we shall consider the word "restrictions." The framers of the Constitution have not qualified the word "restrictions" by the word "reasonable." But the High Court Division has said that the word "reasonable" has to be read with the word "restrictions." The High Court Division has said that "It goes without saying that any restriction imposed by law must be a reasonable restriction otherwise it will negate the right conferred on a citizen by Article 31 of the Constitution. The right conferred by Article 42 must be a meaningful right. We are therefore, of the opinion that restriction imposed by law within the meaning of Article 42(1) of the Constitution must be reasonable restriction although the word 'restriction' is not qualified by the word 'reasonable' as otherwise it would be arbitrary." We are in agreement with the High Court Division that the "restrictions" as spoken about in article 42(1) must be reasonable. At the same time, we hold the view that "Any restrictions imposed by law" as contemplated in sub-article (1) of article 42 of the Constitution clearly contemplate about an of a Parliament and this will be clear if we see the provisions of article 31 thereof which reads as follows:</u>

<u>31. To enjoy the protection of the law, and to be treated in accordance with law, and only in accordance with law, is the inalienable right of every citizen, wherever he may be, and of every other person for the time being within Bangladesh, and in particular no action detrimental to the life, liberty, body, reputation or property of any person shall be taken except in accordance with law.' Is interpreted to mean any law passed by Parliament; art. 31 will cease to be a fundamental right as such an interpretation takes away the entrenchment on the power of Parliament which is the quintessence of a fundamental right and such an interpretation will make a non-sense of the entrenchment by art. 26. Furthermore, it is a requirement of the concept of rule of law that the law must be reasonable and not arbitrary and the Constitution seeking to establish rule of law, the framers cannot be taken to have used the expression 'law' in art. 31 in a sense which com-ports with the concept of rule of law. Art. 21 of the Indian Constitution provides that there shall not be any deprivation of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law'. In the beginning, the Indian Supreme Court refused to import the concept of reasonable and non-arbitrary 'procedure established by law.' Subsequently, relishing that such an interpretation is inconsistent with the provisions of art. 21 as a fundamental right, the Indian Supreme Court held that 'procedure established by law' must mean reasonable and non-arbitrary procedure and not any procedure that may be prescribed by Parliament. Thus in order to preserve the integrity of art. 21 as a fundamental right, the Indian Supreme Court virtually imported the concept of due process as is known in the American jurisdiction.</u>

24. Admittedly, the law or pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law including the one under vicinage is not an act of Parliament as contemplated in sub-article (1) of article 42 read with article 31 of the Constitution. As correctly said by the High Court Division, the basis of law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is the saying of the great Prophet (saw) that "Neighbour has a right superior to that of a stranger in the land adjacent to him." (We shall discuss later on about the legal status of the saying of the great Prophet (saw)). And this law was there on 4th November, 1972 on which day the Constituent Assembly adopted, enacted and gave the Constitution to the people of Bangladesh.

25. In the context, we consider it very relevant to refer to articles 7(2) and 26 of the Constitution and we quote the articles for ready reference.

"7(2). This constitution is, as the solemn expression of the will of the people, the supreme law of the Republic, and if any other law is inconsistent with this Constitution that other law shall, to the extent of the inconsistency be void."

"26.(1) All existing law inconsistent with the provisions of this Part shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, become void on the commencement of this Constitution.

(2) The State shall not make any law inconsistent with any provisions of this Part, and any law so made shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.

(3) Nothing in this article shall apply to any amendment of this Constitution made under article 142.

26. From a reading of article 7(2) and 26, it is clear that any law inconsistent with the Constitution that law and all existing law inconsistent with the provisions of Part III thereof shall to the extent of such inconsistency be void on the commencement of the Constitution. And now we are to see whether the right of pre-emption including the one on the ground of vicinage as recognized in the Muhammedan Law in inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution and the fundamental rights as guaranteed in Part III thereof. And to see this, we are to take the aid of the meaning of law as per the Constitution. According to article 152(1) of the Constitution:

"law" means any Act, ordinance, order, rule, regulation, bye law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage, having the force of law in Bangladesh."

27. Now, in the light of the definition of "law", as in article 152 of the Constitution, we have to consider whether the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage can be said to be a law.

<u>28. The High Court Division observed that the law of pre-emption was not an "Islamic Institution" or "a Quaranik Law." However, as stated hereinbefore, the High Court Division observed that the concept of pre-emption on the vicinage was based on the saying of the great Prophet (saw) "Neighbour has a right superior to that of a stranger in the land adjacent to him." So, naturally, a question arises what is the status of the saying of great Prophet (was) in Islam and its impact amongst the Muslim? To see this, we have to see what Hadith it:</u>

<u>Hadith, Arabic Hadith ("News" of "Story"), also spelled Hadit, record of the traditions or sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, revered and received as a major source of religious law and moral guidance, second only to the authority of the Qur'an, the holy book of Islam. It might be defined as the biography of Muhammad Perpetuated by the long memory of his community for their exemplification and obedience. The development of Hadith is a vital element during the first three centuries of Islamic history, and its study provides a broad index to the mind and ethos of Islam.</u>

<u>From Hadith comes the Sunnah refers to the actions and statements of the Prophet Muhammad (s) as well as tacit approval of the statements and actions of others. The Qur'an and the Prophet Muhammad (s) were sent down by Allah for the benefit of the whole of the mankind for all time. "Sunnath" (literally, a well-trodden path"-i.e., taken as precedent and authority or directive), to which the faith to which the faithful conform in submission to the sanction that Hadith possesses and that legalists, on that ground, can enjoin.</u>

<u>The strength of Hadith is established by the Quran. The Quran is the direct verse of Allah, and Hadith is the refection or narration of the verse of Allah in the words of Prophet Muhammad(s).</u>

<u>From the recital of Shadadah "there is no God but Allah, Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah. The Qur'an makes it abundantly clear that the function of the Messenger is not merely that of a deliveryman who simply delivers the revelation from Allah to us. Rather, he had been entrusted with the most important take of explaining and illustrating the same. This is a point mentioned in a number of verses in the Qur'an:</u>

<u>[And we have revealed unto thee the Remembrance that thou mayst explain to mankind that which hath been revealed for them, and that haply they may reflect.] (Sura An-Nahl 16:44).</u>

<u>[And We have revealed the Scripture unto thee only that thou mayst explain unto them that wherein they suffer, and (as) a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe.] (sura An-Nahl 16:64).</u>

<u>Therefore, Hadith explains, clarifies, and removes ambiguities about the Qur'an. Hence, once we reject the Hadith, we may never be able to figure out the whole meaning Qur'an. Much of Islam will remain mere abstract concepts without Hadith. We would never know how to pray, fast, pay, zakah, or make pilgrimage without the illustration found in Hadith, for these acts of worship remain as abstract imperatives in the Qur'an.</u>

<u>The Qur'an tells us the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) has taught not only the Book but also the wisdom (See Qur'an: 96:2; 33:113, etc.) As Imam Shafi'i stated, the wisdom mentioned here is the Sunnah of Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him); so if we were to reject the Hadith, we would be rejecting the Qur'an itself. The Qur'an tells us to obey the Messenger and abide by his decision: [But no, by the Lord, they can have no (real) Faith, until they make the judge in all disputes between them, and find in in their souls no resitance against Thy decisions, but accept them with the fullest conviction.] (Sura An-Nisaa 4:65).</u>

<u>[So judge between them by that which Allah hath revealed, and follow not their desired, but beware of them lest they seduce thee from some part of that which Allah hath revealed unto thee. And if they turn away, then know that Allah's Will is to smite them for some sin of theirs. Lo! Many of mankind are evil-livers.] (Sura Al-Ma'idah 5:48).</u>

<u>[Your comrade erreth not, nor is deceived; Nor doth he speak of (his own) desires. It is naught save an inspiration that is inspired]. (Sura Al-Nazam 26;2, 3, 4).</u>

<u>[And whatsoever the messenger giveth you, take it. And whatsoever he forbidden, abstain (from it)]. (Sura Al-Hashor 27:70).</u>

<u>It is to be noted that Hadith got three classifications on the basis of qualification-sound (sahih), good (hasan), or weak (da if). The sound (sahib) and good (hasan) basically got the authority of recognized source of law. By the end of the 3rd century it was very much necessary to solidify Hadith into a stable corpus of material to which no new element could credibly be added and from which extravagances had been purged. The Hadith tradition within the various traditions had by them become a permanent and disciplined element in the authority structure of Islam the second great source of law and practice, complementary to the Qur'an and available for analogical handling (qiyas) and for consensus (ijma) as further sources of legislation, arguing from the Qur'an and the Sunnah as primary. For getting sound (sahih) and good (hasan) Hadiths there several compilations. But only six collections, known as al-kutub as-sittah ("the six books"), arranged by matn -those of Al-Bukhari (d.870), Al-Muslim (d.875), Abu Da'ud (d.888), At-Tirmidhi (d.892), Ibn Majah (d.886), and An-Nasai (d.915) -came to be recognized as canonical in orthodox Islam, though the books of Al-Bukhari and Al-Muslim enjoy a prestige that virtually eclipses the other four.</u>

29. The above has been summarized from the books of various Islamic scholars (Hadith hereinafter shall be referred to as Hadis).

30. From the above, we can easily and definitely say that saying of the great Prophet (saw) is Hadis.

31. Let us see the source of pre-emption as Shafi-I-Jar, i.e. vicinage from Hadis: (I) Narrated by Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (saw) said, "Whoever has land and wants to sell it, let him offer it to neighbour (Ibn Majah)." (II) Narrated by Abu Rafi "That the Prophet (asw) said, "The neighbour has more right to property that is near (Sahih Al Bukhaei and Al Muslim)." (III) Narrated by Sharid Bin Suwaid that "I said, 0 Messenger of Allah, (what do you think of) land owned by only one person but this land has neighbours?" He said: "The neigbour has more right to property is near" (Sahih Al Bukhari). (IV) Narrated by Samarah that the Prophet of Allah (PBUH) said, "The neighbour of the house has a greatest right to pre-empt the house" (Jamai of Tirmizi).

32. So, there is no doubt that the source of pre-emption (Shufa) on the ground of vicinage is from sahih Hadis.

33. Now, the next question is whether the Hadis: "Neighbour has a right superior to that of a stranger in the adjacent to him" has assumed the character of law within the meaning of article 152 of the Constitution. My answer is straight and simple and that is a big 'Yes'. Because the law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage is in vogue in this part of the region including Bangladesh for centuries and this right of pre-emption is being practiced by the Muslims, and it, in fact, has become a part of personal law of the Muslims, so it is a law within the meaning of article 152(1) of the Constitution.

34. The question of pre-emption under Mohammedan Law came up for consideration before this Court in the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed @ Tufa Mia and others (supra). In that case while tracing back the history of law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law, this Court stated that

"The law of 'Shafa' has been developed out of the some 'hadises' (tradition) of the Prophet of Islam. Its foundation seems to be based on the principle that all members of the society should attempt to preserve joint nature of their ancestral property. It may appear to be contrary to the modern idea of freedom of alienation of property, and so it is considered as a restriction on the right of ownership. But this law, in some form or other has been prevalent almost in every part of the world since the ancient time, but it is difficult to trace its origin. In all those countries the Law of pre-emption was not developed as a scientific exposition of substantive law, but the Mohammedan Law of pre-emption is highly developed and a scientific exposition of a very difficult branch of law. The Mohammedan Law of pre-emption contains well defined principles restricting the individual rights of property and yet is in complete harmony with principles of equity, justice and good conscience in this filed of law Imam Abu Hanif and disciples have left a unique and distinct mark on the theory of jurisprudence. The right of pre-emption arises only out of a valid, complete and bonafide sale. It does not arise out of gift (hiba), sadaqah, wakf, inheritance, bequest or a lease even though in perpetuity. The right does not arise also out of a mortgage even though it may be by way of conditional sale. Under the Mohammedan Law a sale is an exchange of property for property, the exchange consisting in payment of price by the purchaser to the vendor and delivery of possession by the vendor to the purchaser. Under the Mohammedan Law execution of instrument of sale is not necessary to complete the sale; the sale is complete with the passing of consideration and delivery of possession."

35. From the above quotation, it is clear that the right of preemption under the Mohammedan Law assumed the character of law and in fact, it is stated so in all the books of all the authors of Islamic jurists who have written the Mohammedan Law including Hedaya.

36. It appears that the High Court Division although in its judgment considered the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed @ Tufa Mia abd others (supra) in connection with the question of limitation in filing the suits, it did not notice the above quoted paragraph of this Division. The High Court Division was obliged to look into the above quoted observation of this Court in view of the provisions of article 111 of the Constitution.

37. Mr. Tabarak Hossain, learned Counsel, for the respondent, conceded that the right of preemption under Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage as well as on other grounds is practiced in this region, now Bangladesh, right from ancient period as observed by this Division in the above mentioned case. At the risk of repetition, we state that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage having emanated from Hadis and having been practiced since from time immemorial in this region has become a law within the meaning of article 152 of the Constitution. Further if we see article 152 of the Constitution and article 42(1) thereof side by side, it would appear that the right to acquire, hold, transfer, or otherwise disposal of property is subject to the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law including the one on the of vicinage.

38. The High Court Division has said that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is an unreasonable restriction as it puts restriction upon a citizen either in the matter of acquiring property or holding and/or in the matter of transferring the property. The reasons assigned by the High Court Division in holding so are that if there were no law of pre-emption, a vendor would be entitled to sell his property to anybody at a reasonable price that could be settled between him and the purchaser and that the right to terms for property freely is clearly restricted by law of pre-emption which in many cases result in depression of the price which the vendor could otherwise be able to get for his property, is absolutely imaginary and fallacious. Because the right of pre-emption accurse Only after the transfer/sale of a property, (see the case of Md. Dewan Ali-Vs-Md. Jasimuddin and others, 13 MLR (AD) 2008, 198) so when the price is negotiated, the future right of pre-emption of the adjacent owner can never be a bar on the owner of a property to sell his property at a reasonable price. Our experience never shows that since a Muslim neighbor has a right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage the proper price is not fetched. Rather our experience shows that in order to defeat the right of pre-emption irrespective on the ground of vicinage sometimes higher price is mentioned in the deed than the actual price. Besides, in all cases of sale the neighboring owners do not go to enforce the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage. Another reason shown was that the right if pre-emption "also imposes a restriction on a citizen to acquire a property." This reasoning is also fallacious. The law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law as shafi-I-Jar itself does not create a bar in acquiring a property by a citizen. An owner of a vicinage can never put a hindrance upon a citizen to purchase a property, in other words, a citizen is free to acquire a property, but subject to the right of pre-emption of vicinage of a Mohammedan if he at all chooses to exercise the said right by making the talabs, namely, Talab-i-Mawasibit and Talab-i-Ishad subject to the provisions of article 42(1) of the Constitution. In taking the above view, the High Court Division followed double standard in that it totally forgot that the same thing might happen in case of pre-emption on the right of Sharik-I-Sharik(a co-sharer in the property) and Shafi-I-Khalit (a participator in immunities and appendages such as a right of way of a right to a discharge water); the High Court Division sis not declare the right of pre-emption on grounds of Shafi-I-Sharik and Shafi-I-Khalit ultra vires the Constitution.

<u>39. The other reasons assigned by the High Court Division in the above respect are absolutely beyond the periphery of the fundamental rights and are based on mere surmises and conjectures and based on sound judicial principle and so those are not required to be met by this Court. Moreso, in holding that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage is an unreasonable restriction in acquiring, holding and transferring a property by a citizen, the High Court Division failed to consider that the Muslims of this region have been exercising the right of the pre-emption on the ground of vicinage for centuries and nobody either of the Muslim Community or the Hindu Community of part of the region ever raised any question that the right put unreasonable restrictions in acquiring, holding and transferring a property. In the written statement, on pleading to that respect was also token. The learned Judges themselves also found so, when they observed "It surprises us that neither during the Pakistani days nor even after the emergence of Bangladesh, the constitutionality of pre-emption law in the ground of vicinage has been challenged before this Court." The above fact prima-facie proves that the citizens accepted the right of pre-emption of the Muslims under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage as the personal law of the Muslims. When the framers of the Constitution in Part III thereof clearly recognized "any restrictions imposed by law" that restrictions must be subject to the law of pre-emption on the vicinage as recognized in the Mohammedan Law. And in deciding the question of reasonable restriction put by law, we must remember that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law is not an act of Parliament and this law has emanated from the Hadis of the Prophet (saw) as discussed earlier which has become part of personal law and that is protected by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution which has clearly mandated that every citizen has the right of profess, practice or propagate any religion. But the High Court Division totally failed to consider the status of Hadis and its impact in the personal law as envisaged in article 41(1)(a) discussed above. In the context, we must state that the reasonableness to any restriction imposed by law comes only when a law is enacted by the Parliament. In the context, we find it quire appropriate to quote another passage from the Constitutional Law of Mr. Mahmudul Islam. The passage reads thus:</u>

<u>"When it is said that substantive due process requires a law to be reasonable, the question arises: reasonable in relation to what? The American Supreme Court evolved that concept of 'police power', which is a short description of the inherent power of the State to promote the general welfare of the community, and judged reasonableness of laws in relation to the police power of the State. But the question still remains as to whose conception of reasonableness is control-that of the legislator or that of the court? "In a very famous footnote in United States V. Caroline Products Co." the court articulated the idea that different constitutional claims be subject to varying levels of review." Rational basis test involves a relaxed scrutiny. Under it a law will be upheld if it is found rationally related to a legitimate government purpose. Intermediate scrutiny involves a deeper scrutiny than rational basis test and under it the law will be held valid if it is substantially related to an important government purpose. The third level of scrutiny is strict scrutiny in which case the government to sustain the validity of a law must show that law is necessary to achieve a compelling government purpose. It is level of scrutiny selected by the court that principally determines the fate of a particular case. If the court applies rational basis test, a law or action is very likely to be found valid, while a case attracting the strict scrutiny, the law or action is most likely to be found invalid as the government can hardly show that the law or action subseries any compelling interest."</u>

<u>40. We consider the rational basis test, the most appropriate basis to test the reasonableness of a law and the law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the basis of vicinage is quite rational. As already stated hereinbefore, this law has emanated from the Hadis and being practiced by the Muslims of this part of the region for centuries. Further under the Mohammedan Law, a sale is an exchange of property for property, the exchange consisting in payment of price by the purchaser to the vendor and delivery of possession by the vendor to the purchaser. It is also to be kept in mind that under the Mohammedan Law execution of instrument of sale is not necessary to complete the sale, the sale is complete with the passing of considerations and delivery of possession. And the moment the suit is decreed, the defendants, i.e. the purchaser shall be entitled to get the price of the transferred land, so the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is quite rational. Another test of reasonableness of the law is whether the law is arbitrary. The law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage cannot be said to be arbitrary as well, because if the suit is decreed, the defendant vendee shall get the money back which he paid for the purchase of the property. The right of pre-emption including the one as Shafi-I-Jar having been emanated from the Hadis, every Muslim has the right to practice the same and in Bangladesh, it has always been regarded as a part of personal law, i.e. the Mohammedan Law and that right is guaranteed by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution to. And the right of pre-emption including the one on the ground of vicinage as recognized in the Mohammedan Law is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution and the fundamental rights as guaranteed in Part III of the Constitution.</u>

41. The High Court Division was also wrong in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is discriminatory because though a Muslim can exercise the right of pre-emption as Shafi-i-Jar in respect of a non-agricultural land, a Hindu cannot inasmuch the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law including the one on the ground of vicinage has become part of personal law as discussed above and such right is protected by article 41(1)(a) of the Constitution. Further the Hindus and the Muslims are two different communities and they form two different classes as well and they follow two different religion and faith. The law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage having been emanated from the Hadies of the great Prophet (saw) and having been practiced so long cannot be said to be discriminatory. In the context, the High Court Division has totally misread and misconstrued the provisions of article 28 of the Constitution vis-à-vis 41(1)(a) thereof. Further the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage can be availed of by any Muslim, no discrimination has been made or attempted to have been made by the State between the Muslims. The right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage can be available of by any Muslim irrespective of his status/position in the society. The reasoning of the High Court Division is also fallacious for another reason that so far as the Muslim women of this part of the region are concerned, they inherit from the father whereas, a Hindu woman in this region including Bangladesh does not inherit from the father because of the Hindu Law, i.e. the personal law. So it cannot be said that Hindu Women are being discriminated with the Muslim women. The High Court Division was totally wrong in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage "affects the secular nature of the Republic" inasmuch as the State has not made any discrimination against any citizen in availing the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage between the Muslims and the Hindus, but it is because of the personal law which has been guaranteed in sub-article (1)(a) of article 41 as discussed above.

42. The High Court Division was not at all justified in saying that the right of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law is opposed to the principle of justice, equity and good conscience inasmuch as in saying so it totally ignored the observation of this Court in the case of Shamsuddin @ Tufa Mia and others (supra); in that case, this Court considered the principle of Mohammedan Law and clearly observed that "the Mohammedan Law of preemption contains well defined principles restricting the individual rights of property and yet is in complete harmony with principles of equity, justice and good conscience." In overlooking the above quoted observation, the High Court Division was totally oblivious about article 1 1 1 of the Constitution.

43. From the trend of the impugned judgment, it appears that in holding that the right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage puts an unreasonable restriction upon a citizen in acquiring, holding and transferring a property, the High Court Division relied upon the case of Bhau Ram -Vs- Baij Nath Singh and others heard along with two other appeals, AIR 1962, Supreme Court, 1476 without considering that in the said cases the question of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law on the ground of vicinage was not involved. And in those cases. The constitutionality of certain provisions of the pre-emption laws prevailing in the States of Madya Pradesh (Rewas-State area), Delhi and Maharashtra (Berar area) such as, Rewa State Pre-emption Act, 1946 section 10, in particular, Punjab Pre-emption Act I of 1913, section 16 in particular and section 174 under Chapter XIV of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928, were challenged. In those cases, the Supreme Court of India held the statutory or the customary right of pre-emption based on vicinage as unconstitutional on the main ground that before enactment of those laws, there were no practices or customs for pre-emption in those parts of India. Interestingly in the said cases, the Supreme Court upheld the validity of the right of pre-emption based on co-ownership and on certain appendages, such as a common staticase or a common entrance. Regarding vicinage, the Court held that "we are of opinion that even the law of pre-emption creates a right which attaches to property it would be creating a restriction so far acquiring, holding or disposing of property is concerned which was not there before the law of pre-emption was enacted. Therefore, even if the liability attaches to the property, it will still amount to a restriction on the right guaranteed by Art. 19(1)(f), when it attaches to the property by the law of pre-emption." The reason shown in upholding the right of pre-emption on the claim of co-shareship was that though the law giving such a right imposed a reasonable restriction was in the interest of the general public. In the context, it is very pertinent to state that clause (f) of article 19(1) which was interpreted in the above decision, was omitted by the Constitution (44th Amendment) Act, 1978 and the three cases were decided on 7th March, 1962. The High Court Division failed to notice the fact of omission of clause (f) from article 19(1) of the Indian Constitution in 1978. In relying upon this case, the High Court Division also failed to notice the most notorious fact that before enactment of those laws for pre-emption there was no custom or practice of pre-emption in those parts of India whereas, the law of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage was very much there in Bangladesh for centuries.

44. We conclude that the High Court Division was totally wrong in holding that "Muslim Law of pre-emption so far it relates to the town property was void" and that the right of preemption under the Muhammedan Law based on vicinage, i.e. Shafi-I-Jar was void as it offended the provisions of article (42(l) read with article 31 of the Constitution and being discretionary as well within the meaning of article 28 thereof.

Now the merit of the suits:

45. So far as the finding of the High Court Division as to non-performance to Talabs, namely, Talib-l-Mowasibat and Talab-I-Ishad is concerned, it being the last Court of fact, exhaustively considered the evidence and gave clear finding that the plaintiffs failed to prove Talib-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishad. We have gone through the evidence. We find nothing wrong with the said finding of the High Court Division. Mr. Khan also failed to show any misreading and non-consideration of any material evidence by the High Court Division in coming to the evidence and came to the finding that the plaintiffs performed the talabs. Considering the evidence, we are constrained to concur with the High Court Division that the plaintiffs failed to prove the Talabs as per the Muhammedan Law.

46. So far as the finding of the High Court Division as to the failure of the plaintiffs in proving their ownership of 'B' scheduled land is concerned, though they (the plaintiffs) filed the khatians only before the Courts below to prove their ownership, in this Court, they have filed all the relevant title documents by filing additional paper book to prove their ownership therein. We Wave perused the title documents and these documents prove that the plaintiffs have got title in 'B' scheduled land and as such, we find that the plaintiffs proved their ownership of 'B' scheduled land which is contiguous to the suit land.

<u>47. Another important question decided by the High Court Division was that out of the two plaintiffs, plaintiff No. 1 was a Company and it being a juridical person, it could not profess Islam. Therefore, it could not invoke the right of preemption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage. The High Court Division further found that though plaintiff No .2 was a natural person and he could file the suit under the Muhammedan Law claiming preemption on the ground of vicinage, he did not specify the land out of schedule-'B' of which he was to owner. We are in agreement with the High Court Division that plaintiff No.1 being a juridical person, it could not profess Islam and therefore, it could not pray for preemption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage and as such, the suits for pre-emption at its instant was not maintainable. Since plaintiff No. 2 did not specify 'B' scheduled land in which portion he was the owner, the High Court Division rightly found that the suits at the instance of plaintiff No. 2 was not maintainable.</u>

<u>48. The High Court Division dismissed the suit on the further findings that the right of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage alone will not lie in the case of large estates and is available only when either houses or small portion of holdings of land are transferred; pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law was to prevent the inconveniences which might result from the introduction of disagreeable stranger as a co-partner or near neighbor, its object being to prevail possible vexation arising from disagreeable neighbor; right of pre-emption, therefore, cannot be enforced in the case of commercial lands. These findings are based on sound judicial principle of law as emanated from the Hadis discussed hereinbefore. In this regard, the High Court Division rightly noticed that in the instant case, the plaintiffs sought pre-emption of the suit land comprising a vast area of 8.69 acres though they were the owners of 2.58 acres land and that the plaintiffs themselves set up industry in 'B' scheduled land. The High Court Division further found that though the suit land was recorded as agricultural land, the admitted position was that in the vicinity of the suit land industrial units were established and that the vendee purchased the suit land for setting up industry. We concur with these findings of the High Court Division and hold that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get the decree in the suit on the ground of vicinage.</u>

<u>49. The High Court Division was also correct in holding that the suits were filed long after the completion of sale as per the Muhammedan Law. In this regard, the High Court Division rightly relied upon the case of Shamsuddin Ahmed (Supra). In this case, this Court after evaluating the various decisions including the one of the Privy Council held that under the Mohammadan Law for a valid sale, execution of an instrument of transfer was not necessary. Alter negotiation, the moment the vendor accepts the consideration and puts the vendee into possession, sale is complete, and it gives rise to the right of pre-emption is not dependent on the completion of sale by registration of the instrument of sale. We have no reason to take a contrary view in this case. In the instant case, the agreement for sale vide Ext- 'A' was executed on 16.08.1995 and part payment was made on the date and physical possession of the suit property was also handed over to the vendee on receipt of full consideration, the sale deed was executed and presented for registration on 07.03.1996 whereas, the suit was filed on 30.06.1997, i.e. much beyond the period of limitation of 1(one) year as provided in article 10 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act. But the trial Court totally ignored the above factual and legal aspects of the case and thus erred in law in holding that he suits were not barred by limitation.</u>

50. The High Court Division was also correct in holding that the suits were not maintainable inasmuch as after the transfer in question the vendee had already sold .04 acre land to one Serajul Islam who was made defendant No.3 in the suit, but neither in the plaint nor in the deposition of PW 1 any statement was made to the effect that Talib-I-Muwasibat and Talab-I-Ishad were made in respect of the said .40 acre land.

<u>51. Conclusion: Though we find that the High Court Division was totally wrong in declaring the right of pre-emption under the Muhammedan Law on the ground of vicinage both agricultural and town property void being discriminatory and violative of article 42(1) read with article 31 of the Constitution, the appeals are dismissed for other reasons discussed hereinbefore.</u>

End.
